scenes.name: Electrónica casera: The Normal y Mute
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Contagiado por las Desperate Bicycles, Daniel Miller compra un Korg usado y graba en su cuarto «T.V.O.D.»/«Warm Leatherette» como The Normal: electropunk de puñaladas de sintetizador y erotismo de accidentes de coche a lo Crash de Ballard. Vende treinta mil copias y le convierte en director de Mute (Fad Gadget). A mediados de 1978 coinciden otros singles electrónicos lo-fi de sellos indie: «United» de Throbbing Gristle, Extended Play de Cabaret Voltaire, «Being Boiled» de The Human League, «Paralysis» de Robert Rental y «Private Plane» de Thomas Leer, hecho sin sintetizador y susurrado para no despertar a su novia.

scenes.name: Punk electrónico
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: «Hazlo tú mismo, pero con sintetizadores»: el punk aporta energía y autogestión, y los Korg y Roland japoneses abaratan la tecnología. Daniel Miller funda Mute con The Normal («un cruce entre Ramones y Kraftwerk») y la banda fantasma Silicon Teens; siguen Fad Gadget, Robert Rental, Thomas Leer y DAF.

podcast.title: Creator of The Normal and "Warm Leatherette" (1978)
podcast.body: Daniel Miller was the driving force behind the group The Normal, and he crafted the song "Warm Leatherette" (November 1978) by drawing inspiration from Kraftwerk, Lou Reed, and Giorgio Moroder. This composition contributed to the emerging "cold wave" sound. "Daniel Miller, who's the guy behind the normal, took some elements of craft work, Lou Reed and George Eomeroder, to create this."

podcast.title: Founder of Mute Records
podcast.body: Daniel Miller founded Mute Records using the funds he earned from his unexpected hit single, "Warm Leatherette." His vision for Mute was to create an "all synthesizer label," a focus that proved highly successful as keyboard-driven music gained traction on British charts after 1981. "Daniel Miller, who took the money he made from a surprise hit single of his called Warm Leatherat and founded an independent record company called Mut."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founder of Mute Records
podcast.body: After the success of his bedroom-recorded single "Warm Leatherette" (selling up to 25,000 copies), Miller used the earnings to establish Mute Records, conceptualized as a label exclusively for synthesizer bands. "This made Daniel enough money to follow an idea he had. What if there were a record label that released nothing but music by synthesizer bands? He called his label Mut and one of the very first bands he signed was a group from Basil in England who had recently thrown away all the guitars and had bought synthesizers."

xref.title: Production of "I Feel Love" (1977)
xref.body: Giorgio Moroder produced Donna Summer's 1977 track "I Feel Love," which became known as the first truly computerized and synthesized dance single. His work on this track incorporated elements that later influenced artists like Daniel Miller of The Normal. "That was the first truly computerized, slashed synthesized dance single, which she created with the help of producer George Eomeroder."

xref.title: Bedroom Punk Aesthetic with Synthesizers
xref.body: Daniel Miller, aspiring to be a punk but unable to play guitar, bought a Korg 700S and a 4-track reel-to-reel machine from his film editor savings. He recorded "Warm Leatherette" in his bedroom, creating a minimalist, futuristic sound with attitude, which sold 30,000 copies. This demonstrated that musical experience wasn't necessary for creating impactful electronic music, embodying a punk sensibility of DIY attitude over traditional ability. "He started experimenting with it in his bedroom. Recorded two songs, found some money to make a test pressing and convinced the rough-trade record shop in Notting Hill to stock it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bedroom Recording Pioneer
xref.body: Daniel Miller, the sole member of The Normal, composed and recorded the single "Warm Leatherette" in his bedroom in 1978, showcasing the accessibility of electronic music production. "Daniel Miller, the solitary member of a band known as The Normal from 1978 with Warm Leatherette, a single that became a substantial UK hit that year, and a song that was composed and recorded in Daniel's bedroom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Founding Mute Records
xref.body: Using the profits from "Warm Leatherette," Daniel Miller established his own independent record label, Mute, dedicated exclusively to guitar-less music, which later introduced artists like Depeche Mode, Erasure, and Yazoo. "He took the profits and founded his own independent record label devoted entirely to guitar less music. He called the label Mute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Funding Mute Records Expansion
xref.body: The money generated from the sale of 30,000 copies of The Normal's seven-inch single, "Warm Leatherette," was reinvested by Daniel Miller into Mute Records, which eventually led to his collaboration with Depeche Mode. "Daniel took the money from that single Warm Leatherette by The Normal and plowed it back into mute, which eventually saw him cross paths with Depeche Mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Minimalist Sound as a Contrast
xref.body: The minimalist sound of Daniel Miller's "Warm Leatherette" served as a benchmark against which the later, more sonically advanced and textured Technopop songs from 1980-81 were compared, highlighting the rapid technological progress in a short period. "Remember what warm leatherettes sounded like? Now compare that minimalism to something like this, which came out less than two years ago."
